question_text: Find $k$ given the consecutive arithmetic terms:

mark_breakdown.desc: Equating differences of consecutive terms: $k - 3 = 11 - k$

subparts.solution:
If $3, k, 11$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence, then
$k - 3 = 11 - k$ {equating differences}
$\therefore 2k = 14$
$\therefore k = 7$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: For three consecutive terms $a, b, c$ in an arithmetic sequence, the common difference is constant: $b - a = c - b$, which means $b = \frac{a+c}{2}$.
step_by_step: Set up the equation equating differences: $k - 3 = 11 - k$.
Add $k$ to both sides and add 3 to both sides: $2k = 14$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Subtracting terms in inconsistent orders, such as $3 - k = 11 - k$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Equate the differences between successive terms: $u_2 - u_1 = u_3 - u_2$, then solve the resulting polynomial equation.
step_by_step: Simplify the right side: $k^2 + 11 - k - 4 = k^2 - k + 7$.
Move all terms to one side: $k^2 - k + 7 - k - 6 = 0 \implies k^2 - 2k + 1 = 0$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting brackets around $(k + 4)$ when subtracting it on the right side.

mark_breakdown.desc: Equating the consecutive differences for an arithmetic sequence: $2k - (k - 5) = 2k^2 - 2k$

subparts.solution:
If $k - 5$, $2k$, $2k^2$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence, then:
$$2k - (k - 5) = 2k^2 - 2k \quad \{\text{equating differences}\}$$
$$k + 5 = 2k^2 - 2k$$
$$2k^2 - 3k - 5 = 0$$
$$\therefore k = -1 \text{ or } \frac{5}{2} \quad \{\text{using technology}\}$$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: In an arithmetic sequence, the difference between any two consecutive terms is constant: $u_2 - u_1 = u_3 - u_2$.
step_by_step: Set up the common difference equation using consecutive terms: $2k - (k - 5) = 2k^2 - 2k$.
Solve the quadratic equation by factoring $(2k - 5)(k + 1) = 0$ or using a graphics calculator to find $k = -1$ or $k = 2.5$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Sign error when expanding $-(k - 5)$, incorrectly writing $-k - 5$ instead of $-k + 5$.
